turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Tuesday, the twentieth of October. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
[curious] Three up top. Paris has put a curfew on the Place de la République after half a million people marched.
[wry] A central bank in Taipei is loosening the clamp while a state fund quietly pre-positions rescue money.
[deadpan] And six guitars were built identical except for the back wood, and nobody could hear the difference.
There's one thread through all of that. Start in France.
Saturday the seventeenth. A nationwide day of action. The interior ministry counted five hundred and fifty thousand marchers, a hundred and ten thousand of them in Paris.
And the organisers?
Eight hundred thousand. Around twenty-four hundred people were arrested.
Wait — what started this?
Schools. It began on the twenty-first of September as a protest about conditions in one Paris borough.
[curious] And that becomes half a million people?
It fused with fuel prices, food prices, and a revived yellow-vest strand. The budget is the trigger — the prime minister is taking the deficit from five point four per cent of output to five.
[exhales] And the president?
Addressed the country on Sunday. His words: those who destroyed must pay, those who looted must reimburse. He said the country felt anger and shame.
Did anyone resign?
The interior minister offered. Macron refused it — the Élysée said he wanted the chain of command intact.
And then he left the country.
[deadpan] And then he left the country. Monday, a four-nation Gulf tour. Kuwait, the Emirates, Bahrain, Qatar.
For what?
Oil and diesel. The Élysée's own phrase was alternative and bypass routes.
[scoffs] So the president whose streets are burning over fuel prices flies to the Gulf to ask for fuel.
That is the whole issue in one sentence, and it's why the spine today is the pass-through.
Meaning what, exactly?
One energy shock, and all the different doors it comes out of. Here's the number. American energy prices rose twenty point four per cent in the year to September.
[thoughtful] Twenty per cent. That's not a line item any more.
It's most of a three point seven per cent headline inflation print. Which is why the Federal Reserve is still raising into a slowing economy.
Still raising. That's the part people keep getting wrong.
Target range three and three quarters to four per cent, after a quarter-point increase on the seventeenth of September.
And the market?
Monday is the thing to sit with. Global equities fell. Global bonds fell. Every Treasury yield rose.
[curious] Both legs at once.
Both legs at once. That's diversification failing, and failing for exactly the reason it's supposed to.
Explain the mechanism — because most people think bonds are the airbag.
They are, for a growth scare. If the economy slows, yields fall, bond prices rise, and the bond leg cushions you.
Right.
This isn't a growth scare. It's a supply shock. Energy gets more expensive, inflation rises, so yields rise — and bond prices fall at the same time equities do.
So the airbag deploys backwards.
BlackRock named it in April. Supply-side disruptions, they wrote, can have the opposite effect, with bond prices falling and yields rising.
[thoughtful] Okay. And gold? Gold's supposed to love this.
Gold fell. Six tenths of a per cent, to about four thousand one hundred and forty dollars an ounce.
During a shooting war in the world's main oil chokepoint.
During exactly that. With the ten-year at five point one five, the cost of holding something that pays you nothing beats the safe-haven bid.
[drawn out] Huh. And bitcoin?
Up about one per cent, on China's growth print. It traded as a risk asset, which is what it is.
Let's do the chokepoint, because you mentioned it. Hormuz.
The body that counts the attacks has effectively said it can't.
[skeptical] Say that again?
UKMTO. It now states plainly that its own tally understates what's happening, because most of the targeted vessels have stopped reporting to it at all.
So every number we've printed on this story is a floor.
Every number is a floor. Its week to the sixteenth logs at least twelve ships attacked, and two hundred and fifty-four transits.
Against what, normally?
About a hundred and thirty-five a day before the war. So call it thirty-six.
[thoughtful] So a third is gone and two-thirds still moves.
That's the honest middle between Tehran saying closed and the American commander saying it's controlled by the United States and its partners.
And the cost of going through?
That's where the war is legible. War-risk cover was a quarter of one per cent of hull value before this. It's now six to ten.
Put that in money.
Up to about twenty million dollars for a single supertanker voyage into the Gulf.
[exhales] Right. Singapore. Same shock, different door?

Same shock, completely different instrument. On Monday the government accepted the National Wages Council's guidelines: six to eight per cent for workers earning up to two thousand eight hundred dollars a month.
Which is who, exactly?
The twentieth percentile of full-time citizens. Last cycle was five and a half to seven and a half, at a lower threshold.
So it's gone up. What's actually new?
A fourth category. For the first time there's a recommendation for employers who did not perform well and are loss-making — at least a hundred and twenty dollars.
[skeptical] And how many employers followed the last set?
This is the number. One outlet reports slightly more than a quarter met last year's recommendations.
A quarter.
A quarter. And we flagged it in print as single-sourced, because it appears in no other account we read, including the ministry's own release.
[wry] But if it holds, a recommendation isn't a pay rise. It's a press release.
Only the Progressive Wage Model and the Local Qualifying Salary are actually enforceable.
And the contrast is right there in the same week, isn't it.
The same ministry charged seven employers and an administrative assistant for declaring CPF contributions for local employees who didn't work for the companies.
Phantom locals.
To inflate foreign-worker quota. Where that ministry has a statute, it prosecutes. Where it has a guideline, it urges.
What about the haze? It's been running for weeks.
The map has flipped. At five this morning the west was the island's worst region — a hundred and twenty-two — and the only one still unhealthy.
And the north? That was the bad one.
Eighty-eight, and the cleanest. Central read two hundred and twenty-five on the sixteenth, so it's a hundred-point fall island-wide in four days.
Incomplete, though.
Incomplete. And the agency issued three more preventive-measure notices on Monday — ten companies now.
Technology. What did Beijing actually do?
Something sharper than the headlines said. Three days after proposing its AI export list, it shipped finished, dated, enforceable controls on tunnel boring machines and dredger parts.
[curious] Boring machines. Not chips.
Effective the eighteenth of November. Meanwhile the AI catalogue is still a consultation draft taking comments until the fifteenth.
So the glamorous one is a draft and the unglamorous one is law.
That contrast is the story. And we owed readers a correction on the open-source question.
Go on.
Yesterday's issue described the carve-out as a licence Beijing could revoke, attributed to a reader who'd installed Chinese office software to read the original.
And?
No document or analyst we read this week uses revocation language. What the draft actually does is stranger: publishing a model as open source can itself constitute a technology export.
[thoughtful] So publishing is exporting.
The exemption that exists is narrow and backward-looking. It grandfathers what's already public. Everything after that needs a licence.
Fair. And the home lab — this is the bit I know you've been waiting for.
[amused] Reflection released Beam. Five hundred and one billion parameters, twenty-three billion active, Apache licensed.
On what hardware?
Somebody measured it on the eighteenth. One Mac Studio, two hundred and fifty-six gigabytes of unified memory. Twenty-nine tokens a second.
[excited] Wait — a five-hundred-billion-parameter model, on one desktop?
Experts streaming from the internal drive. Peak footprint two hundred and thirty-six gigabytes.
And the big graphics card? The one everyone bought?
[deadpan] The smallest community quantisation is a hundred and three gigabytes. A thirty-two gigabyte card isn't in this conversation.
[laughs] Brutal.
And the thread caught the lab out. They used a puzzle they said was a few days old to show the model wasn't memorising.
Let me guess.
Traced to a post from August of last year. One commenter called the failure to check rather sloppy, and the company conceded and revised the caption.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every morning with this one.
[laughs] What have we got?
Steel bicycle framebuilding. Cutting steel tubes and joining them with heat.
And why today?
Because on Friday the biggest handmade-bicycle show in the world opens in Osaka. First time in Asia. Seventy-plus makers.
[excited] That's a six-and-a-half-hour flight.
Advance tickets closed Thursday. The door costs more.
Okay, so what's the state of this craft?

It has just been through a controlled demolition. Since twenty-twenty it has lost its lug supplier, its tubing importer, both of its major schools, its biggest American parts maker and its biggest British one.
[exhales] That sounds terminal.
Paragon Machine Works ceased major operations in March after forty-three years. Its own words: our business is no longer viable.
And yet the show is expanding.
Here's the turn. In May a Portland company bought Paragon's entire intellectual property — and is releasing the design files free, to keep them perpetually available to independent builders.
[thoughtful] So somebody bought the wreckage and open-sourced it.
And opens a school next month.
What does the material actually cost? I always assume it's the expensive part.
A complete tube kit, delivered, with brazing rod and flux: a hundred and eighty-nine pounds.
That's nothing.
The material is nothing. The hours are everything.
And the sceptic?
Two custom builders charge exactly zero for custom geometry. Pegoretti's own page says there is no extra charge for a custom geometry.
[scoffs] If the bespoke geometry were the hard-won heart of it, it would have a price.
And the man with the most famous waitlist in framebuilding says the tools are a trap. His line: equipment is nice, but it's not a substitute for a procedure.
Can you do any of this in Singapore?
[deadpan] No. No school, no hobbyist brazing class, nowhere to run an acetylene torch. In a flat that's not a hobby, it's a fire-safety incident.
[laughs] Noted. Stay with the craft theme — the Atelier.
Acoustic guitars. And there's a published blind test that is quietly devastating.
Tell me.
Six steel-strings built to one design, varying only the back and sides. Brazilian rosewood, Indian rosewood, mahogany, maple, sapele, walnut.
And?
Thirty-one guitarists tested them in dim light wearing welder's goggles. The finding: guitarists could not easily distinguish the guitars by their sound or feel.
[gasps] The back wood is inaudible?
The paper's phrase is a marginal impact. Now hold that against a price list. One luthier charges about eighteen thousand US dollars to change the back to Brazilian rosewood.
And the top?
About five hundred and fifty to change the top to Adirondack.
[deadpan] And the top is the part you can actually hear.
The top is the radiator. Collings now grades its tops by measured damping — they strike a billet with a steel ball and listen with precision microphones.
So the expensive upgrade is the inaudible one.
That's the line. And there's a white-label truth underneath it. Bourgeois is an Eastman company.
Meaning?
Their Touchstone tops are voiced in Maine, then sent to Eastman's workshop in Bazhou, China, to be built into guitars. Same designer, same voicing, same name on the headstock.
What's the price difference?
At one dealer, on one day: three thousand two hundred and ninety-nine dollars, against six thousand seven hundred and forty-nine for the Maine build.
[thoughtful] A third of the price. And in this climate?
Singapore owners have solved it themselves — air-conditioning the case down to fifty-five per cent, or reactivatable silica. The failure here is bridge glue creeping, not cracking.
Against the number one film?
Street Fighter took eight thousand six hundred and seventy-one per screen, from three and a half thousand of them.
[laughs] Four to one. What is it?

Footage William Greaves shot in August nineteen seventy-two at Duke Ellington's home in Harlem, on sixteen millimetre. Surviving figures of the Harlem Renaissance, many of whom hadn't seen each other in fifty years.
And he never finished it.
His son did. A hundred per cent from fifty-five critics.
[warmly] That's lovely. Although — two screens.
[deadpan] Two screens is not a verdict. It's one New York opening weekend. The test is whether it holds when it expands.
Family desk — she's twelve now.
A study of three thousand four hundred and eighty-six children who did not have a phone at twelve, followed to thirteen.
What happened?
Symptom scores moved about a tenth of a standard deviation. School-night sleep fell. Screen time rose.
That's small.
That's small. The large number is different: the odds of owning a social media account were three point two times higher.
[thoughtful] So the phone isn't the thing.
The phone is the delivery vehicle. The payload is an account and a lit screen at bedtime — which carried the largest coefficient in the whole paper.
And what didn't move?
Academic performance. Exercise. Bullying. None of them.
So the intervention is the bedroom, not the screen.
And a second study this month found that owning a phone was associated with better sleep. It was using it in bed that wrecked it.
[exhales] That's a much more useful instruction than ban the thing.
Fitness, briefly. Five hundred and sixty-two thousand adults. Each additional metabolic equivalent of fitness, sixteen per cent lower hazard of death.
[excited] Sixteen per cent per unit?
[deadpan] And the actual gain in the model's ability to discriminate risk was two one-hundredths.
[laughs] Okay, that's a cold shower.

And the sceptic is sharp. Eric Topol points out that nearly all the outcome data comes from treadmill fitness, not from measured oxygen uptake — and that wearables underestimate it in fit people and overestimate it in unfit ones.
So the number on my ring is not the number in the paper.
Not the number in the paper.
Close it out. The Long Read.
Taiwan. And a borrowed word — rotten-tail building. It's what mainland China calls a tower abandoned halfway up.
And Taiwan spent years explaining why it was immune.
In twenty twenty-two a state-bank executive said there was nothing to fear, because you need only hand it to another developer.
What changed?
In Taiwan you buy a flat that doesn't exist. You pay in stages against construction progress for two or three years, and take the mortgage only at handover.
[thoughtful] So the buyer is the construction lender.

Unsecured, and ranking behind the statutory mortgage on the building. And the market stopped clearing. Cancellations ran four in twenty twenty-two; three thousand four hundred and fifty-seven in seven months of this year.
And the safety net?

Built and dismantled. In nineteen eighty-six Taiwan created a licensed escrow-modelled industry, banks required to hold a third of each firm. In two thousand and three the rule was repealed on a technicality and never replaced.
[exhales] So it had been hollow for twenty-three years.

And here's the tell. The central bank says in print that the collapse figures are a press artefact. Then in September it loosened lending limits — and in October a state fund signed a new instrument to pre-position rescue finance for stalled sites.
Governments don't build emergency plumbing for problems they think are imaginary.
Which is the argument. And the buyers have already voted: forty-seven per cent now want a completed home they can see and touch.
[thoughtful] They haven't panicked. They've just stopped lending.
That's the sentence. And the question Taiwan hasn't answered — who finances construction when the households decline — is one every pre-sale market in Asia will be asked.
[exhales] That's the Briefing, then.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
